newsHook: You set out the five priorities airports should be working on in 2026 and you are the only person who sees the capital, capacity and regulatory picture across every ACI region at once, so operators from Bristol to Bismarck want to know which of those priorities you would put money behind first.
questions: Of the five priorities you set for 2026, which one would you fund first if you were running a two million passenger regional airport with a tight balance sheet?
Airports keep telling ACI that capital is the constraint, not demand. What financing models are you seeing work for mid-size operators, and which ones worry you?
Capacity is being added at hubs while regional airports fight for slots and airlines. How should a regional airport make its case for growth capital?
Cost per passenger has risen sharply since 2019. Where do you see airports actually taking cost out rather than passing it on in charges?
Procurement of security and baggage technology is now driven by regulation as much as by choice. How should airports avoid buying kit that is obsolete before it is paid for?
You ran Los Angeles World Airports through the pandemic. Knowing what you know now, what would you have done differently on capital and contracts?
Where does ACI World go from here?

personRole: Principal and Global Aviation Leader, Arup
newsHook: You now lead Arup's aviation business worldwide as well as its Americas market strategy, which means you see how terminal and airfield programmes are being scoped, priced and delivered on both sides of the Atlantic, and airport operators want to know what the well run programmes have in common.
questions: When an airport board asks Arup to make a terminal programme affordable, what is the first thing you take out of the scope and what should never be cut?
How much capacity should a mid-size airport build ahead of demand, and how do you stop a programme being sized for a forecast that never arrives?
Construction costs have moved a long way since 2020. Where do you see airports losing money in delivery, and what contract structures protect them?
Procurement of design and engineering is often price led. What does a client get wrong when they buy on fee rather than on outcome?
You have worked on airports in North America and Europe. What does each side do better, and what should they borrow from each other?
Looking at programmes you have delivered over three decades, what would you do differently if you were the client rather than the engineer?
Where does Arup's aviation business go from here?

newsHook: You are the engineer responsible for taking Gatwick's own operation to net zero by 2030 and making the airfield hydrogen ready, and operators elsewhere want to know what that costs, what pays back and what you would skip.
questions: Net zero for your own operation by 2030 is a hard engineering target. What has been the biggest capital line so far and what has surprised you on cost?
How do you keep a single runway airport running at capacity while replacing plant, power and fuel systems underneath it?
Engineering budgets are the first thing finance teams look at when growth slows. How do you defend maintenance spend against a capex freeze?
How do you procure long life assets like ground power, HVO supply or electrical infrastructure when the technology and the regulation are both still moving?
What has the switch to HVO for airside vehicles actually delivered, and would you do it the same way again?
If you were starting the net zero programme again in 2026, what would you do differently?
Where does London Gatwick go from here?

personRole: Chief Executive Officer, Newcastle International Airport
newsHook: You were named best airport in Europe in your size band, were the fastest growing of the UK's fifteen largest airports in the first quarter, and are building a 60 million pound terminal extension while heading for a record six million passengers, which is exactly the growth story regional airport leaders elsewhere want to understand.
questions: You are spending close to 60 million pounds over two years on a terminal extension and arrivals hall. How was that funded and how did you make the case to your shareholders?
Nineteen new routes in one year is a lot for a regional airport. What did you offer airlines to win them, and how do you know the growth will stick?
You are adding more than 30 per cent security processing capacity at peak. What did that cost per lane and how did you choose the equipment?
How do you keep the terminal working for record numbers while it is a building site?
Regional airports are often price takers with airlines and with suppliers. Where have you managed to change that?
What has gone wrong in the expansion so far, and what would you do differently next time?
Where does Newcastle International Airport go from here?

personRole: Chief Executive Officer, Kelowna International Airport
newsHook: You opened the first 108 million dollar phase of a terminal expansion in January that is funded entirely from airport revenues and improvement fees, with no taxpayer money and a municipally owned airport, which is a financing model every mid-size airport leader wants to hear more about.
questions: The whole 422 million dollar programme through 2033 is being paid for from airport revenues and the Airport Improvement Fee. How did you structure that and what did the City of Kelowna need to see before it said yes?
What made you sequence the departures lounge, security checkpoint and food and beverage first rather than gates or apron?
Being the largest municipally owned airport in Canada means council makes the final call. How does that change the way you plan capital and manage risk?
You went for CATSA Plus CT screening in the new checkpoint. How did you work with a national screening authority on equipment you do not own?
Mass timber and a local Okanagan identity are unusual choices for a terminal. Did they cost more, and did they pay back commercially?
What would you do differently on phase one before phase two starts?
Where does Kelowna International Airport go from here?

personRole: Joint CEO and Chief Operating Officer, Vienna Airport
newsHook: You completed a 25 million euro rollout of 35 CT scanners across every checkpoint in July, in time for the summer peak and while holding an average security wait of around five minutes, and operators facing the same EU mandate want to know how you did it without the queues other airports have seen.
questions: Thirty five CT units for 25 million euros is a big single purchase. How did you run the procurement and what did you specify beyond the regulation?
Many airports that installed CT saw throughput fall before it rose. How did you avoid that, and what did the operating cost per lane do?
What did the rollout mean for security staffing and training, and did you need more people or fewer?
You are also building Terminal 3 for 2027. How do you decide what to spend on the existing terminals when a new one is coming?
As joint CEO and COO you sit between the operation and the shareholders. Where do you push back on capital requests from your own operations team?
What would you do differently if you were running the CT programme again?
Where does Vienna Airport go from here?

personRole: Chief Executive, Regional and City Airports
company: Regional and City Airports (Bournemouth, Exeter and Norwich)
newsHook: You grew passengers 23 per cent across three small UK airports in one year, took Bournemouth to a record 1.39 million passengers and a 21 per cent rise in cargo, and lifted Exeter by 32 per cent, which is the kind of turnaround leaders of struggling regional airports want to hear explained in detail.
questions: Small regional airports have been closing or shrinking for a decade. What did you change at Bournemouth and Exeter to get 26 and 32 per cent growth in a single year?
How do you allocate capital across three airports of very different sizes, and who loses when the budget is tight?
Bournemouth's cargo is up 21 per cent. What does cargo do for a passenger airport's economics, and what did you have to build to win it?
What does it cost you to win a new airline base or route, and how do you decide when the incentive is too expensive?
Running three airports lets you share procurement, systems and people. Where has that actually saved money and where has it not?
Looking back over the last three years, what would you do differently?
Where does Regional and City Airports go from here?
